terms.short: The program that starts the talk and asks for something.
The program that waits for a client and answers it.
A link from your computer back to itself. No bytes leave the machine.
A small piece of data. One byte holds a number from 0 to 255.
A way to write bytes with the digits 0 to 9 and the letters a to f.
The path that carries bytes between two programs.
A list of everything that happened, in order.
One line in the trace. It records one step, such as bytes sent.
A value made with a private key. Anyone with the public key can check it.
A signed card that ties a name to a public key.
Certificate authority. A signer that clients agree to trust.
A root certificate the client trusts from the start. Other trust grows from it.
The opening talk where two programs agree on keys and check each other.
A signed note that says who the holder is and what the holder may do.
A fresh signed proof sent with a token. It shows the sender holds the token's key.
Someone who listens to the wire but takes no part in the talk.
Data that anyone can read.
Data scrambled by a key. It looks like random noise.
A value that locks, unlocks, signs, or checks data. A shared key and a private key are secret.
One shared key locks and unlocks the data. Both sides hold a copy.
A key pair: a private key that stays with its owner, and a public key that anyone may have.
A standard lock for data. It scrambles data in 16-byte blocks with a secret key.
terms.strength: Equal to the key size: 128, 192 or 256 bits.
terms.statusNote: AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 are acceptable for encryption and decryption.

terms.short: A chunk of 16 bytes. AES locks data one block at a time.
A random starting value that makes each locked message differ, even under the same key.
A number used once. Each message under one key needs a new one.
A mode that locks each block alone. Equal blocks give equal results, which leaks patterns.
terms.keySizes: The key size of the block cipher it runs, such as AES.
terms.strength: n/a, see strengthNote
terms.strengthNote: It hides each block, but equal blocks stay equal, so the pattern of the data shows.
terms.statusNote: SP 800-38A still lists ECB. The draft SP 800-131A Rev. 3 disallows it for encrypting secret data and keeps it for legacy use.

terms.short: A mode that mixes each block with the one before it, so repeats look different.
terms.keySizes: The key size of the block cipher it runs, such as AES.
terms.strength: n/a, see strengthNote
terms.strengthNote: It hides the data, and it needs an unpredictable IV. It does not catch changes, so it needs a separate seal such as HMAC.
terms.statusNote: SP 800-38A specifies it. TLS 1.3 dropped it: every TLS 1.3 cipher suite is an AEAD mode such as GCM.

terms.short: A mode that locks data and adds a tag that catches any change.
terms.keySizes: The AES key: 128, 192 or 256 bits. The nonce is 96 bits in TLS.
terms.strength: n/a, see strengthNote
terms.strengthNote: The strength of the AES key, while each nonce under one key is used once. A repeated nonce can expose the data and let an attacker forge tags.
terms.statusNote: SP 800-38D specifies it, with a strict rule that IVs stay unique under one key (section 8). TLS 1.3 must implement TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256.

terms.short: A short seal sent with a message. The receiver checks it to catch changes.
A function that turns any data into a fixed-size fingerprint. A tiny change alters it fully.
A seal made by hashing a message together with a secret key, in two rounds.
terms.keySizes: Any length. Keys of 112 bits or more are acceptable for making a seal.
terms.strength: Up to 256 bits, with SHA-256 and a 256-bit key.
terms.strengthNote: The key length and the hash set the strength.
terms.statusNote: FIPS 198-1 specifies it. Keys shorter than 112 bits are disallowed for making a seal.

terms.short: A seal made from a block cipher such as AES and a secret key.
A way for two programs to reach a shared secret while others listen.
The public half of a key exchange. It is safe to send in the open.
A key exchange built on lattice math, meant to resist quantum computers.
terms.keySizes: Three sets: ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024.
terms.strength: n/a, see strengthNote
terms.strengthNote: NIST security categories 1, 3 and 5. The course runs ML-KEM-768, category 3, paired with X25519.
terms.statusNote: FIPS 203 specifies it (August 2024).

terms.short: A key exchange that runs two methods together. An attacker must break both.
A new kind of computer that could break some of today's key exchanges and signatures, such as X25519.
A scheme where every sale gets its own key, made from a base key and a counter.
terms.keySizes: AES DUKPT: AES-128, AES-192 or AES-256 base keys. The course runs AES-128. An older form uses TDES.
terms.strength: n/a, see strengthNote
terms.strengthNote: Each sale key is used once, so one leaked sale key exposes one sale. A leaked base key exposes every reader's keys, because the bank derives every reader key from it.
terms.statusNote: ANSI X9.24-3-2017 specifies AES DUKPT. Its free test-vector supplement says AES DUKPT derives keys from AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 initial keys.
terms.reasoning: The strengthNote is reasoning from how the keys are derived.
terms.unsourced: The TDES form of DUKPT, and its status, cite no source in this draft. The full X9.24-3-2017 text, which ANSI sells, was not read.

terms.short: The base derivation key. A bank keeps it and uses it to rebuild each reader's keys.
Key serial number. It holds the reader's id and a counter, and travels with each sale.
A PIN packed with the card number into a fixed-size block, then locked.
Sending a copy of an old message again, hoping the receiver accepts it.
Memory that the .NET runtime controls. It may move and copy objects on its own.
Code meant to take the same time whatever the secret data is.
A chart that counts how many timings fell in each range.
A number that compares two groups of timings. A large size means they differ by more than noise.
The part of a compiler that rewrites code to run faster. It can change timing.
A modern way to sign things. Its keys are short and the signatures are small.
terms.keySizes: 32-byte private key, 32-byte public key, 64-byte signature.
terms.strength: About 128 bits.
terms.statusNote: RFC 8032 specifies it. FIPS 186-5 approves EdDSA. A draft NIST plan disallows today's signatures, Ed25519 included, after 2035, because a quantum computer could break them.

terms.short: A text file that holds a key or a certificate between two marker lines.
A key pair method that can sign and can lock a small secret for one owner.
terms.keySizes: 2048 bits or more. 3072 bits for 128-bit strength.
terms.strength: 2048 bits gives 112 bits. 3072 bits gives 128 bits.
terms.statusNote: RSA signatures are approved in FIPS 186-5. Sending a key with old PKCS #1 v1.5 padding is disallowed after 2023. TLS 1.3 removed RSA key transport. A draft NIST plan deprecates 112-bit RSA after 2030 and disallows RSA after 2035.

terms.short: An older key pair method that only signs. It cannot lock data.
terms.keySizes: 2048 or 3072 bits (L), with a 224- or 256-bit q (N).
terms.strength: 2048 bits gives 112 bits. 3072 bits gives 128 bits.
terms.statusNote: FIPS 186-5 no longer approves DSA for making signatures. It may still check old signatures.

terms.short: A key pair method on elliptic curves that only signs. It cannot lock data.
terms.keySizes: P-256, P-384 or P-521 curves.
terms.strength: P-256 gives 128 bits. P-384 gives 192 bits.
terms.statusNote: FIPS 186-5 approves it. TLS 1.3 must support ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256. A draft NIST plan disallows it after 2035.

terms.short: A way for two sides to agree on a shared secret in the open. It does not sign or lock data.
terms.keySizes: A prime of 2048 bits or more. 3072 bits for 128-bit strength.
terms.strength: 2048 bits gives 112 bits. 3072 bits gives 128 bits.
terms.statusNote: Approved at 2048 bits or more. TLS 1.3 removed static DH and keeps only fresh keys per session. A draft NIST plan disallows it after 2035.

terms.short: Diffie-Hellman on an elliptic curve. It agrees a shared secret with small keys.
terms.keySizes: P-256 or P-384 curves, or Curve25519 (see X25519).
terms.strength: P-256 gives 128 bits. P-384 gives 192 bits.
terms.statusNote: Curves of 224 bits or more reach 112 bits. TLS 1.3 must support key exchange with P-256. A draft NIST plan disallows it after 2035.

terms.short: ECDH on Curve25519. It agrees a shared secret with 32-byte keys.
terms.keySizes: 32-byte private key, 32-byte public key.
terms.strength: About 128 bits.
terms.statusNote: RFC 7748 specifies it. TLS 1.3 should support it. A quantum computer could break it, so the course also pairs it with ML-KEM.

terms.short: An old lock with a 56-bit key. A brute-force search finds the key.
terms.keySizes: 56 bits.
terms.strength: Below 80 bits. SP 800-57 lists no strength row for it.
terms.statusNote: NIST withdrew FIPS 46-3 on May 19, 2005, because DES no longer provides the security needed for Federal information. In July 1998 the EFF DES Cracker found a 56-bit key in 56 hours, on a machine that cost well under $250,000.

terms.short: DES run three times with two or three keys. Also called Triple DES or TDEA.
terms.keySizes: 168 bits (three keys) or 112 bits (two keys), counting 56 bits per key.
terms.strength: Three-key TDES gives 112 bits, not 168. Two-key TDES gives 80 bits.
terms.statusNote: Two-key TDES encryption is disallowed. Three-key TDES encryption was deprecated through 2023 and is disallowed after 2023. Decryption with either form is allowed for legacy use. SP 800-67 Rev. 2, its standard, was withdrawn on January 1, 2024.

terms.short: An old stream lock. Its output has biases that leak the data.
terms.keySizes: Variable. The RFC 6229 test vectors run from 40 to 256 bits. TLS used 128 bits.
terms.strength: n/a, see strengthNote
terms.statusNote: RFC 7465 says TLS clients and servers must never negotiate RC4, in any TLS version.
terms.unsourced: TLS used 128 bits: this rests on the TLS suite names, which this draft did not reread.

terms.short: A modern stream lock. TLS pairs it with Poly1305 to catch changes.
terms.keySizes: 256 bits. The nonce is 96 bits and the Poly1305 tag is 16 bytes.
terms.strength: 256 bits, by RFC 8439 section 4. SP 800-57 lists no row for it.
terms.statusNote: RFC 8439 specifies ChaCha20-Poly1305. TLS 1.3 should implement TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256.

terms.short: A hash with a 32-byte output. Anyone can compute it, so it needs a key to become a seal.
terms.keySizes: No key. The output is 256 bits.
terms.strength: 128 bits against collisions. 256 bits inside HMAC.
terms.statusNote: FIPS 180-4 specifies it.

terms.short: A way to turn one shared secret into several separate keys, built on HMAC.
terms.keySizes: Takes any secret. Gives keys of the length asked for.
terms.strength: n/a, see strengthNote
terms.strengthNote: No more than the secret it starts from and the hash it uses.
terms.statusNote: RFC 5869 specifies it. HMAC-based key derivation is acceptable to NIST.

fieldNotes.kind: symmetric, asymmetric, hash, mac, kdf, mode or scheme.
fieldNotes.does: encrypt, sign, agree-key, hash, mac or derive-key. A method that does not list encrypt cannot lock data.
fieldNotes.strength: Security strength in bits, as NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 counts it. The key size and the strength often differ. n/a means strength is not a number of bits here, and strengthNote explains.
fieldNotes.status: current, legacy or broken. Legacy means old data may still be read or checked, and new protection must not use it.
fieldNotes.statusBasis: final when a published standard states the status. draft when only a draft states it.
fieldNotes.lessons: Lessons where the engine runs the method. namedIn lists lessons that only name it.
fieldNotes.strengthNote: Prose about strength, used when strength is not a number of bits.
fieldNotes.reasoning: A claim that follows from how the method works, with no citation. In the comparison, an item marks this with basis: reasoning.
fieldNotes.unsourced: A claim in the entry that cites no primary source yet.

symmetric.meaning: One shared key locks and unlocks. Both sides hold the same key.

strengths.text: Short keys reach high strength. AES-128 gives 128 bits. RSA needs 3072 bits for the same 128 bits.
NIST does not expect to replace today's symmetric standards for quantum computers.
Modes such as GCM lock the data and catch changes in one step.

weaknesses.text: Both sides must hold the same key before they start. That key must travel safely, or be agreed first.
Each pair of people needs its own key. Ten people need 45 keys: each person pairs with 9 others, and each pair counts once (10 x 9 / 2).
A shared key cannot show which side made a message. A MAC shows only that it was computed by the party or parties sharing the key.

asymmetric.meaning: A key pair. The private key stays with its owner. The public key may go to anyone.

strengths.text: Two strangers can start in the open. Only public values travel, and the private key never leaves its owner.
A signature made with a private key can be checked by anyone who holds the public key, so it shows who signed.

weaknesses.text: Keys are larger for the same strength: RSA-3072 and P-256 both give 128 bits, the same as AES-128.
A public key proves nothing alone. An attacker can swap in a public key of their own. A certificate chain to a trusted root ties the key to its owner.
A large quantum computer could break RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA, DH and ECDH. NIST's draft plan disallows them after 2035.

asymmetric.notAllEncrypt: Not every key pair method locks data. DSA, ECDSA and Ed25519 only sign. DH, ECDH, X25519 and ML-KEM only agree a key. RSA can sign and can lock a small secret.

myth.claim: The private key is never shared, so asymmetric encryption is more secure.
myth.truth: Keeping the private key at home removes one risk: moving a secret. It does not make the lock stronger. AES-128, RSA-3072 and P-256 all give 128 bits. A stolen private key lets the thief act as its owner. A stolen key that unlocks data opens everything locked to it. A public key with no proof of owner lets an attacker stand in the middle.

steps: Agree a key: each side sends a key share, such as X25519 or X25519 with ML-KEM-768. Both sides compute the same secret. Fresh shares each session give forward secrecy.
Prove who you are: the server signs the handshake with its certificate key, such as Ed25519, ECDSA or RSA. The client checks the certificate chain to a trusted root.
Make the keys: HKDF turns the shared secret into separate keys for each direction.
Lock the data: AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 locks every record and catches changes.
tlsUsesBoth.why: The key pair methods solve the start: agreeing a key with a stranger and proving who you are. The symmetric lock then does the bulk work with short keys.
